summary: FireTrack is a web-based platform that harmonizes fire hotspot data from NASA’s MODIS and VIIRS sensors, addressing differences between datasets to provide a more consistent historical view of fire activity. It combines records dating back to 2003 through spatial and temporal processing and sensor calibration, aiming to reduce duplicate detections and improve comparability. The platform offers an interactive map with filters for region, period, and fire intensity based on Fire Radiative Power (FRP), a historical fire activity calendar, and a dashboard showing hotspot totals, historical averages, and anomalies. Users can also export filtered data for further analysis. By turning satellite observations into accessible information, FireTrack supports environmental monitoring, early warning strategies, and emergency response planning. Rather than predicting fires, it helps identify critical periods and unusual activity, providing authorities and environmental managers with information to anticipate risks, plan interventions, and strengthen preparedness while promoting informed decision-making, data literacy, and environmental protection.
details:
FUNCTIONS AND OBJECTIVES

FireTrack is a web application that harmonizes hotspots detected by two satellite sensors provided by NASA FIRMS: MODIS, which has a longer historical record and a spatial resolution of approximately 1 km, and VIIRS, with a resolution of 375 m, capable of detecting smaller hotspots. The platform combines these detections into a consistent historical time series covering the period from 2003 to November 2026. Rather than simply combining CSV files, the system groups detections that are close in space and time to reduce double counting, counts cells in an H3 hexagonal grid with detections per day, and calibrates MODIS data to the VIIRS scale during the period of simultaneous observation by both sensors. Within this period, approximately 14.1 million detections were processed. In validation using a held-out year, the calibration achieved R² = 0.986 at the monthly scale and R² = 0.76 at the daily scale. For other regions, the platform already provides near-real-time (NRT) hotspot monitoring, while the loading of their respective historical records is still underway.

With this structure, users can select a region and a time period to view a calendar organized by year and month, with colors representing the intensity of fire activity, as well as an interactive map developed with Leaflet and a dashboard featuring indicators such as total hotspots, historical averages, and anomalies. These metrics include the percentage deviation and percentile of the analyzed month in relation to the same period in previous years. The platform also allows users to filter data and export it in CSV format, as well as download the calendar as a PNG.

FireTrack's main objective is to support environmental monitoring, emergency response, and territorial management by providing organized and accessible information to firefighters, inspection and environmental agencies, researchers, and scientists. The platform also seeks to contribute to environmental education and data literacy in school settings. By providing information on fire activity, the system supports decision-making and expands access to relevant data for protecting communities and populations with greater difficulty accessing information. Informational Telegram alerts, aimed at residents and firefighters, are already available and also contribute to this purpose. The project is aligned with Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) 13 and 15 through the monitoring of fire activity and its environmental impacts; SDG 4 through the promotion of education; SDG 17 through data dissemination and sharing; and SDGs 11 and 3 through the provision of alerts that support community safety and the protection of life.

BENEFITS AND DISTINCTIVE FEATURES OF FIRETRACK

The project was developed with environmental factors and the impacts associated with climate change in mind, seeking to provide tools that contribute to monitoring fire activity and improving response strategies. Through FireTrack, managers, researchers, and emergency response teams gain access to a more consistent overview of hotspot occurrences over time, without having to interpret products from different sensors separately.

One of the platform's main distinguishing features is its fire activity calendar, organized by intensity-based colors, which makes it possible to quickly identify seasonal patterns, critical periods, and unusual behavior. The system also offers intensity filters based on Fire Radiative Power (FRP), using classes calculated individually for each sensor to avoid inappropriate comparisons between different scales. Another important feature is the availability of data in CSV format, allowing it to be reused in research and other applications. In addition, the platform includes accessible color palettes, including options adapted for people with color vision deficiencies and high-contrast modes, making information interpretation more inclusive.

Another distinguishing feature is the forecast of fire activity for the next seven days, generated by a LightGBM statistical model with isotonic calibration. In the tests conducted, the model achieved a ROC-AUC of 0.87. The results are accompanied by plain-language explanations generated with the assistance of artificial intelligence, making the information easier to understand for different audiences. In this process, generative AI is used exclusively to interpret and explain the results and is not responsible for generating the forecasts.

ABOUT OUR PROCESS, ASPECTS, AND RESOURCES

The project was developed using official data provided by NASA through the FIRMS system, including records from the MODIS and VIIRS sensors, with data from the NOAA-20, NOAA-21, and Suomi NPP satellites. Artificial intelligence tools, such as OpenAI ChatGPT and Claude, were used to support research, requirements organization, and textual and technical review. Development assistants, such as Claude Code, also provided support during certain implementation stages, while the project's conception, validation, and development decisions remained the responsibility of the team. The main resources used and their respective purposes are listed below:

  • Data: NASA FIRMS (MODIS and VIIRS, including NOAA-20, NOAA-21, and Suomi NPP).
  • Processing: Python, pandas, H3, scikit-learn, and LightGBM.
  • Database: PostgreSQL, hosted on Supabase, and SQLite during testing.
  • API: FastAPI.
  • Orchestration: Workflows documented in Apache Hop, available in the project's `hop/` folder. However, there is no confirmation that they were executed in an actual installation of the tool.
  • Front-end: Next.js, TypeScript, Tailwind CSS, shadcn/ui, Recharts, Leaflet, and OpenStreetMap.
  • Design: Figma and v0, for developing the platform layout.
  • Forecasting: LightGBM with isotonic calibration.

No specialized hardware was required to develop the platform.

During the process, certain criteria were established to ensure the proper interpretation of the data. A hotspot does not necessarily represent a confirmed fire, just as two detections considered coincident do not necessarily correspond to the same event. Likewise, FRP-based intensity must be interpreted according to the characteristics and scale of each sensor.

The team also prioritized the use of updated data, including information from the NOAA-20 and NOAA-21 sensors in near real time. The most recent historical data, particularly those covering the period from August to November 2026, are still undergoing additional validation. While the historical time series from 2003 to November 2026 is available, other regions have near-real-time monitoring and are still receiving the loading of their respective historical data.

Finally, FireTrack was designed to promote accessibility and the dissemination of environmental information, keeping the platform open for data consultation and visualization. Users interested in receiving notifications can register through a form, and alerts are delivered via Telegram. These notifications are informational in nature and support decision-making; they do not replace official emergency procedures. In situations involving risk, users should contact their local emergency number.
